content: I walk into the starport bar on Regina and look for my contact, the broker Ines Varga.

The Reginald Station bar smells of recycled air, cheap stimulant, and the faint ozone tang of the docking clamps outside. Fluorescent panels flicker overhead, casting a sickly amber glow over the scatter of pilots, mechanics, and dockworkers hunched over their drinks. A low thrum of the station's gravitic field vibrates through the floor in your boots — the *Kestrel* is still clamped on the far side of the deck, her drive coils ticking as they cool.

You scan the room. Two-thirds empty, standard mid-shift lull. And there, in a corner booth with a single chair pulled back, sits a woman in a grey travel jacket unbuttoned over a fitted black shirt. Dark hair cut short and practical. A pair of hands resting on the table, fingers long and still, nails trimmed to functional stubs. She's watching the room's single security camera with the quiet, patient attention of someone who's done it a lot.

She catches your eye. Nods once. Not a smile. An acknowledgment.

You cross the floor. The chair slides out without being asked.

"Captain Sorel." Her voice is low, clipped, no wasted syllables. Accent you can't place — not Regina, not the core worlds you've worked before. "Ines Varga. You have the *Kestrel's* manifests current and her survey certificates in order?"

It's not a question. It's a filter.

She taps the table surface with one fingertip, twice, then rests her hand flat. A thin silver band catches the light — no, not a ring. A data-clip, old military spec. She glances down at it as if she forgot it was there, then looks back up, expression unchanged.

"I'll be direct because you have work to do and I don't have time to dance. Three sealed crates. Origin: off-manifest. Destination: a port I'll name when you've accepted the run. Compensation: two thousand credits, paid on delivery, plus fuel allowance. No questions about contents, no scanning, no detours. You fly, I handle the paperwork at each end."

She pauses. Studies your face.

"You're behind on the mortgage. I've seen the filing. I'm not here to mock you. I'm here because the *Kestrel* flies clean and her captain doesn't ask stupid questions in the middle of a run. Those two things are rarer than they should be."

The data-clip catches the light again as she fidgets with it, twisting it around her finger. One eye drifts to the door. Once. Quickly. Back to you.

"So. Are we flying?"
I buy Ines a drink and ask what cargo she has for me.

You wave the barkeep over with two fingers. "A greyhound, double. And one of whatever she's having. If she's having one."

The barkeep squints at you. "Ladies don't usually order here on a Tuesday."

"Then she's unusual."

He slides over a glass of something that looks like it was distilled in a ship's galley and named by a bored intern. You set it down in front of Varga along with your own. She glances at it. Doesn't move.

"Appreciated," she says, flatly. "I'll note the gesture."

Then, because you've asked *what cargo*, her stillness shifts. Not angry. Something colder. A gear engaging.

"Captain. I said *no questions about contents.*" She lets the sentence sit for a beat. Her thumb finds the data-clip on her finger again, turns it once. "I'm going to ask you to hear what I actually mean, not what a port bar's background noise tells you I mean. The crates are sealed. They stay sealed. You don't open them, you don't scan them, you don't describe them to a mechanic, a port authority, or a friend at a dockside. You fly a vector and you deliver a box. That's the entire job."

She picks up the glass. Takes one small, precise sip — the kind a person takes to confirm a taste, not to enjoy one. Sets it down.

"For your manifest, if you need words: *industrial components, prototype grade, non-hazardous.* That's all it is and all you'll ever need to know. The customs stamps I'm carrying match that description. If anyone asks at port, you have a clean manifest and my paperwork. That's the whole of it."

She leans forward slightly. Elbows on the table now. Voice drops half a register.

"You asked because you're a professional and you want to know what you're sitting next to in Realspace. Fair. I'll give you one *operational* fact, because it's your ship and your life. The crates have a mass signature slightly higher than their external dimensions suggest. If your inertial dampeners chug on a jump, it's the cargo, not a miscalculation. Don't worry about it. Don't let your engineer worry about it, because I've seen what happens when curious people start poking at things they were told not to poke at."

A thin, almost-forgivable smile. The first one you've seen on her face.

"Two thousand on delivery. Fuel at four hundred a leg. Three legs. You've got the *Kestrel's* survey current through next month. Oskar's on board, I assume — good, I want him flying quiet. You have her mortgage coming due in nine days, and you're not going to make it on a standard trade run. I know because I've *read the filing.*"

She stands. Buttons her jacket. Leaves the glass — three-quarters full — on the table.

"Docking assignments close in six hours. If you're in, I want a flight plan on the *Kestrel's* comm by then. If you're not, I'd like the drink back for the road."

She doesn't leave. She waits. The data-clip catches the fluorescent light as she taps it against her palm. *Tap. Tap.* Steady. Measured. The rhythm of someone counting something in her head.

The bar's background noise swells and recedes. The barkeep is mopping a spill three tables down, not looking.

The glass sits between you, amber and patient.
Deal. I leave the bar and head back to the Kestrel at bay 12.

The corridor from the bar to bay 12 is a twelve-minute walk through Deck C of Reginald Station. The air gets cooler as you move away from the hab ring, the recycled-molecule hum shifting from muffled to mechanical. Your boots echo on plating that hasn't been re-foamed in a year. You pass a row of sealed cargo holds — some blinking with priority tags, most dark and forgotten — and a pair of dockworkers arguing about shift rotation in a language with too many guttural consonants.

Bay 12.

The *Kestrel* hangs in her cradle like a bird too large for the cage. Mid-range free trader, single hull, drive coils blue-dark in the bay's low lighting. Her paint is scuffed in long grey streaks along the port side, and the docking clamps are still warm, ticking faintly. A small decal on the nose — a kestrel in flight, badly rendered — is half-peeled.

The airlock hisses before you reach it. Oskar is already on the inner side, pulling the manual override. He's a compact man, forearms mapped with burn scars he won't talk about, a shop rag tucked into his collar like a second skin. He's got a torque wrench in one hand and a coffee mug in the other, and his expression is the specific *I-was-not-expecting-this* look of a man who just finished a six-hour coolant-line repair.

"Captain." He steps aside. "You look like you just either won a bet or signed a contract. Those are the same face on you."

He glances past you toward the airlock. Toward the bar. Then back.

"Varga?"

It's not a question. He's heard the name before. The way you say *Varga* in the same flat tone you'd say *mortgage* or *fuel*.

Oskar takes a slow sip of coffee. Sets the mug down on a coil. Sets the wrench down. Crosses his arms.

"Well. You're doing it."

Not *are we doing it*. Not *should we do it*. *You're doing it.* The engineer who kept the *Kestrel* flying through the Kethani dust storm, who rebuilt the starboard drive housing with a plasma cutter and a prayer. He's not asking. He's cataloguing.

"Here's what I need before we go dark." He ticks off fingers. "Manifest. Sealed. I want to see the customs stamps myself, because if I'm flying a cargo bay I want to know the legal shape of what's in it. You told me *industrial components.* Fine. I'll log it as industrial components. But if those crates start putting off a heat signature I don't recognise, or the inertial dampeners start doing *things* on a jump —" He waves a hand. "— I'm the one in the engine room. So I'm the one who needs to know what 'normal' looks like. Can you get me a spec sheet?"

He lets the silence do work.

"Also. Nine days. The mortgage. I did the math while I was fixing the port manifold. Two thousand on delivery, a thousand two in fuel across three legs, that's three-two on the table, minus the bank takes you down to the line. You're not paying this month's payment in full. You're scraping by." He shrugs. "That's your problem. My problem is that the *Kestrel* doesn't jump with a mystery in the cargo hold and no one telling me what the mystery is."

He uncrosses his arms. Leans on the console.

"Where's the first port?"
I run the pre-flight checks with Oskar.

You move through the *Kestrel* in order, top to bottom, fore to aft. Oskar moves in parallel, a beat behind, calling out as he goes. The ship answers you both the way a well-matched pair of hands answers a tune: not perfectly, but *knowably*.

**Cockpit and nav.** You cycle the master bus. The flight display comes up in stages — attitude, heading, fuel, drive alignment. All green. You run the nav computer's self-test; it returns a clean checksum. You check the jump predictor against the local ephemeris for Reginald Station's gravitational well. The numbers line up. You log the time.

Oskar's voice comes over the internal comm from the engine room, a half-second delayed. "Drive coils, port and starboard, at nominal. Spin-up resistance is within three percent of factory spec. You're not going to hear them *sing*, Captain, but they're not going to *scream* either. Which, for a six-year-old free trader, is the whole ballgame."

**Life support.** You pull the environmental panel. O₂ mix at twenty-one point two percent. Pressure at one point zero one atmospheres. Cabin temperature steady. The recycler filters have a week of margin before the next swap — you note it in the log. Oskar confirms from below: "Heater loops are clean. No moisture in the lines. I'd be worried if I heard them hiss and I *don't* hear them, so that's the good kind of silence."

**Hull and clamps.** You release the docking clamps in sequence — port forward, starboard forward, port aft, starboard aft — and watch the bay cameras. The *Kestrel* drifts free on her attitude thrusters with a soft, rhythmic *thump-thump* you feel in the soles of your boots through the deck plating. No asymmetric thrust. No drift. Oskar calls it "textbook" in a tone that means he's already written it up in the maintenance log and will sign it before you can blink.

**Cargo bay.** Here Oskar lags. You open the bay door and look into the empty space — six standard pallet mounts, all empty, all clean. The bay smells of sealed polymer and the faint metallic ghost of the last shipment, which was machine oil and two hundred cases of low-grade stimulant for the Kethani colony. Nothing else. Nothing yet.

"Crates coming today?" Oskar asks from the comm. His voice is a shade flatter than before. Not suspicious. *Awaiting.* The tone of a man who's decided the answer is going to be *yes* and is calibrating how much he cares.

You turn back to the cockpit. Set the departure time in the nav computer. Pull up the fuel manifest: the *Kestrel* has enough reaction mass for two full jumps and a third if you're careful. Enough for the three legs Varga laid out, with a margin you'd call *adequate* if you weren't calling it *bare*.

Oskar surfaces at the cockpit hatch, still in his shop rag, still holding the coffee mug. He sets it down on the console — on the *edge*, the way he always does, as if testing whether it'll slide. It doesn't. He doesn't look surprised.

"Ship's green," he says. "All of her. I'd fly her through a hair dryer with her eyes closed." A pause. He looks at you. "So. You want me to load the crates when they come, or do you want me to *watch* them come in and ask the dock worker some *interesting* questions first?"

He says *interesting* the way other people say *dangerous.*

The bay lights hum. The *Kestrel's* instruments tick softly around you, all green, all waiting. Outside the bay window, Reginald Station turns slowly against the black, its docking fingers blinking amber.

Oskar crosses his arms. "And the first leg. Where are we going, Captain? I need a star to point at."
We lift off, and once we're clear of the planet we jump for the Efate system.

The *Kestrel* pushes clear of Reginald Station on a gentle vector burn, the bay's amber clamps shrinking behind you until they're just two pinpricks in the black. Oskar calls the final attitude check from the engine room. "All green, Captain. Drive alignment is within a degree of the jump vector. You're clear to spool."

You are.

The drive coils spin up in a low, rising whine that you feel in your molars before you hear it with your ears. The nav computer locks the jump corridor. You commit.

Then: nothing. And everything. The stars smear into streaks that smear into *nothing*, a white pressure behind your eyes that lasts maybe a heartbeat and maybe a year. The deck plating groans. The coffee mug Oskar set on the console slides two centimetres to the port side. You do not mention it. He does not mention it. The ship takes the weight the way a good ship takes weight: silently, evenly, without drama.

Then the stars snap back into shape. Hard. Sudden. The nav display flickers, recalculates, and resolves: **Efate system, gravitational well, stable.**

"Realspace," Oskar says from the comm, his voice carrying the specific flat satisfaction of a man whose instruments agree with each other. "Drive coils spooled down clean. No harmonic irregularity. No *singing.*" He pauses. "Whatever we're carrying on this run, it's not aboard yet. Which means this jump was the honest kind. The boring kind." A beat. "I'm going to enjoy the boring kind while it lasts."

You set a parking orbit above Efate Prime. The world fills the viewport: a mottled ochre-and-green sphere, continents the size of your thumb, cloud bands drifting slow as oil. A station — Efate Relay, smaller than Reginald, older, its docking fingers splayed and slightly asymmetric. Two other ships in the traffic lane. A courier with a red stripe. A tug, ugly and broad, towing a dead module.

Oskar surfaces in the cockpit again. He pulls up the local comm frequencies, scans them, and frowns at the readout.

"Standard port traffic. No anomalies. No Varga on the band." He looks at you. "So. You jumped to Efate with an empty cargo hold and a nine-day clock. What's the plan, Captain? Are we meeting her here, or are the crates here, or am I supposed to be surprised?"

He uncaps a pen. Taps it against his lip. The *Kestrel's* instruments tick around you, all green, all patient.

The ochre world turns slowly below. Somewhere in that mottled surface, a port city is waking to its Tuesday.
When we arrive at Efate, I take the shuttle down to the startown and find the buyer's warehouse.

The shuttle ride down is nine minutes of grey atmosphere and the particular vibration of a two-seater that's been refitted three times and never properly. You punch through the cloud layer and Efate's starport unfolds below: a sprawl of corrugated hangars, a single approach tower with a cracked visor, and the kind of tarmac that's been repaved so many times it's more scar than surface. The air that hits the shuttle's skin smells of rust and burnt fuel.

You park in the general-aviation block, engine cooling, and step out into the late-afternoon heat. The starport is smaller than Reginald. Meaner. The people here move with the economy of a town where everything's a walk and nothing's a luxury. A few pilots lean against their ships. A customs officer dozes behind a booth that's more plywood than architecture.

The warehouse Varga's coordinates point to is on the far side of the apron, past a row of defunct cargo pods and a fuel depot that's been dark for weeks. It's a standard industrial unit — concrete, corrugated steel, a loading bay door painted a faded industrial blue. No signage. No company name. Just a number stencilled in white near the entrance: **H-47.**

You're three steps from the door when you hear the voice.

"Captain Sorel."

A man steps out from behind a fuel drum. Mid-fifties, broad through the shoulders, wearing a dockside coverall with the sleeves rolled to the elbow. His face is the kind that's been晒 by tarmac suns and engine exhaust: red-raw, lined, with a scar that bisects his left eyebrow. He's not holding anything. His hands are in his pockets. He's not smiling.

"Varga sent word you'd be here. I'm Matus. I handle the physical side of things." He gestures with his chin toward the loading bay. "Crates are inside. Three. Sealed. Stamped." A pause. He looks at you the way a man looks at a dog that's just sat in a puddle. "I've got a question, and I'm only going to ask it once. Do you want the spec sheet Oskar's going to want, or do you want to load them up and get back in the sky before the sun goes down?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. He turns, walks to the loading bay door, and hits the release. The steel groans upward on pneumatic arms, and the interior light spills out over the apron.

Three crates. Two metres each, stacked in a neat column. Matte black. No labels you can read from here. They sit on a pallet, and the pallet sits on a floor that's been swept clean — *cleaner* than the rest of this warehouse, if that's possible. The light off them is wrong. Not reflective. Not quite. Like the surface is *absorbing* a fraction of the lumens and giving back slightly less. A tiny, almost-imperceptible dimming at the edges.

Matus steps back. "Lift slings are on the rack. You'll need to tag them for the shuttle, or Oskar's shuttle, or whatever you're bringing back. I don't care which. But they go on your manifest the moment they cross that door, Captain. I don't ask what's in them. I've never asked what's in them."

He leans against the doorframe. Arms crossed. Waiting.

The sun is lower now. The shadow of the loading bay stretches long across the tarmac. Somewhere behind you, the shuttle's engine ticks as it cools.

The crates wait.
I hand over the crates and collect the payment.

You step into the loading bay. The crates up close are heavier than they look — the pallet's load readout, when you press your thumb to it, clicks back **4,210 kg** for three units that are two metres on each side. Your cargo manifest lists a theoretical max of 6,000 kg. You're within spec. The number sits in your head like a pebble in a shoe. You file it away.

Matus pulls a manifest tablet from his coverall pocket and taps it twice. "Stamped. Customs-clear for transit through any Imperial port you'll be touching. Origin is listed as *Kethani Industrial Consortium, Batch 7741.* Destination is listed as *Efate Relay, H-47, Captain L. Sorel, Kestrel.*" He looks up. "That's you. That's your ship. That's your manifest. From this second, if a patrol asks, those crates are *yours* until they're no longer."

He sets the tablet in your hand. Cold. Official. The stamps are clean, serialised, unimpeachable.

"The payment." He says it flat, like a fact. Then: "Varga's terms. Two thousand on *final* delivery. Not here. Here, you get the fuel allowance for this leg — four hundred, wired to the *Kestrel's* registry account by now. And a five-hundred deposit, same channel, to keep your mortgage from eating your face while you're in the air." He shrugs. "I'm not the one writing the cheques, Captain. I'm the one handing you boxes. But I will say, for what it's worth, that's more upfront than most of the work I've watched come through this bay."

He presses a small data-chit into your palm. "Final delivery coordinates. She sent them to me an hour ago. Don't open them here. Open them in the cockpit when you've got your bearings and your engine room is quiet." A beat. "And Captain. If the crates start doing things to your nav computer — and I mean *things*, not the usual drift — you don't troubleshoot. You log the reading, you keep flying, and you let the ship do what it does. Oskar's a good man. Good men ask *why.* Let him ask *why* to a screen, not to a crate."

He steps back from the doorframe. The loading bay light hums. The three black crates sit on their pallet, edges faintly dimmer than the rest of the room, patient and sealed.

"Shuttle's in block nine, I assume. Slings are on the rack. You've got maybe forty minutes before the customs shift change and this apron gets crowded with people who ask *very* specific questions about cargo mass discrepancies." He pushes off the doorframe. "Fly clean, Captain."

The sun has dropped lower. The shadow of H-47 stretches across the tarmac like a long, dark tongue. Behind you, the shuttle's engine ticks. The data-chit is warm in your palm.

You have the crates. You have the manifest. You have a deposit in your account and a destination you haven't opened yet. Two legs left. Nine days. The *Kestrel* is waiting in block twelve, Oskar is waiting in the cockpit, and the sky is getting the particular amber colour that means the port will start locking down in about an hour.
I take a cheap room in the startown and sleep. The next morning I go looking for work.

The room costs forty credits. That's the kind of number that tells you everything about Efate: the sheet is thin, the pillow is a suggestion, and the wall between your bed and the next bed is a single layer of something that was once concrete and has since become more *idea* than material. You can hear the man in the next room breathe. You can hear the building's ventilation system wheeze like a lung with a history. You sleep anyway, because you are a captain, and captains sleep when they can, and the *Kestrel* is waiting with three black crates in her hold and a destination sealed in a data-chit in your pocket.

You sleep nine hours. You wake to the sound of a door banging somewhere above you and the smell of coffee that might be coffee or might be a memory of coffee.

---

The morning light through the window is grey and flat. You eat a flatbread from a cart outside the spaceport apron, pay two credits, and walk the two blocks to the **Efate Relay Pilots' Exchange** — a low, wide building with a glass front that's been cracked and re-cracked so many times it's more fracture than pane. Inside: a row of terminals, a half-dead coffee machine, and a wall of job postings that range from *urgent* to *urgent but with a slightly different font.*

You scan the board. Most of it is the usual: cargo hauls between Efate and the three mining stations in the outer system, a fuel shuttle looking for a relief pilot, a survey contract for a geological firm that will pay in credits and in *patience.* None of it will fill the gap between where your account is and where the mortgage wants it by the ninth day.

Then you notice the pinboard on the left wall. Smaller. Less official. The kind of board where the jobs don't get posted to the Exchange because the people posting them would rather not leave a digital trail.

Three postings:

**1.** *"Private hire. Two-person crew. Short run, one leg, good pay. Meeting at Dock 7, 1400 hrs. Ask for Petran."* No ship name. No cargo description. The handwriting is quick, almost angry.

**2.** *"Kestrel, reg EF-7741. Captain Sorel. Urgent. Aldrin Credit Union, port agent: D. Kess. Report to Exchange office B, 1000 hrs."*

The paper for this one is different. Crisp. Printed, not handwritten. The letterhead is clean: **ALDRIN CREDIT UNION — EFATE RELAY BRANCH.** The stamp is red. The word *URGENT* is underlined twice.

**3.** *"Fuel shuttle, 1400 hrs, Dock 3. Relief pilot needed for 6-hr run. 80 cr. Ask for Yuen."*

You stand in front of the board. The coffee machine gurgles. A pilot two seats down from you is reading the *Reginald Gazette* tablet and eating a protein bar with the focused violence of a man who skipped breakfast twice.

The *Kestrel* is clamped in block twelve. Oskar is somewhere in the engine room, probably, doing what Oskar does: checking things, logging things, being quiet and green and waiting for a vector.

The data-chit is in your jacket pocket. Warm. Unopened.

The pinboard waits.
I go to the Scout Service office at the Efate starport to ask about survey contracts.

The Survey & Exploration Licensing office is on the second floor of the starport's administrative block, behind a door that's been painted a different colour in each of the last three administrations. The current colour is a beige so aggressive it's almost a personal insult. The sign above the door reads **EFATE RELAY — SURVEY & EXPLORATION LICENSING** in letters that were once white and are now the colour of old tea.

Inside: two desks. One empty. One occupied by a woman in her late forties with a grey braid pinned up under a headset that hasn't been used since the previous administration. Her nameplate reads **T. OKAFOR — SENIOR CLERK, SURVEY DIVISION.** She's eating something small and orange from a foil wrapper and staring at a terminal with the expression of a woman who has been staring at terminals for a very long time and has made peace with the fact that they will always be staring back.

You approach the desk. She looks up. Looks at you. Looks back at the terminal.

"Survey contracts," she says. Not a question.

"I'm looking for work. Short-term. One or two legs if possible."

She peels the foil wrapper off her fingers and smooths it flat on the desk. "Name and registration."

"Sorel. *Kestrel*, EF-7741."

She types. The keystrokes are slow, deliberate, the way a person types when they'd rather be doing anything else. The terminal chirps. She frowns at it. Types again. Chirps.

"Free trader. Mid-range. Current survey cert expires—" she squints, "—the fourteenth of next month. So you're valid. Good." She pulls up a list. Scrolls. The cursor bounces once, twice, settles. "Right. Here's what's on the board this week."

She reads, in the flat cadence of a woman reading words that do not interest her:

"**One.** Geological soundings, outer system. Mining station Keth-9 to asteroid cluster 4417. Twelve hours each leg. Payload: survey gear, four hundred kilos max. Payout: three-fifty a leg. Minimum two legs. The mining company is *Draxen & Fould*, and I will save you the trouble of asking: they pay in credits, they pay on schedule, and they do *not* tip."

She scrolls.

"**Two.** Atmospheric survey, Efate Prime, northern quadrant. Twelve-day contract. You'd need a certified atmospheric survey team of at least two. Payout is better — two-two-fifty — but you'd be on the surface for twelve days and you'd need to bring your own equipment. I don't think that's what you're looking for."

She scrolls again. Stops.

"**Three.** This one's new. Posted an hour ago. Orbital survey, *private* client. Single leg, Efate to the L2 Lagrange point and back. Fourteen hours. Payout: eight hundred credits, flat. The client's name is redacted. The requirement is: ship must be *unregistered* on the jump corridor. You log the jump locally, you do not file it with the Relay's traffic authority. The client will supply the clearance codes at the dock."

She looks up. The chewing has stopped.

"I'll be plain with you, Captain, because I've been doing this nineteen years and I've seen what happens when people say *yes* to that one without understanding the shape of the *no* that follows. Redacted client. Unfiled jump. That's either a research team that doesn't want the traffic board knowing their schedule, or it's something that doesn't want the *traffic board* knowing their schedule. Those are different sentences. The first one is boring. The second one is a headline."

She folds her hands. The headset cable dangles between them.

"All three are yours to take or leave. The mining one is the safe one. The atmospheric one is the long one. The private one is the one that pays like it's not supposed to." She tilts her head. "What's the shape of the hole you're trying to fill, Captain?"
I accept the survey contract and head back to the Kestrel to tell Oskar.

The walk back to the apron is ten minutes of flat tarmac and the low sun baking the corrugated roofs of the hangar row. The Survey office's beige door is already behind you when you feel the ground change texture — smoother, better-paved, the *Kestrel's* block. You pass Dock 7 where a wiry man with a patchy beard is leaning against a courier shuttle, tapping his foot. You don't stop.

Block twelve. The *Kestrel's* airlock is dark. But the engine room light is on, a warm amber rectangle in the lower port side, and the faint tick of a cooling manifold is audible through the hull.

Oskar is in the engine room when you open the hatch, standing at the coolant coupling with a cloth in one hand and a very small, very precise screwdriver in the other. He's got his back to you. He's been talking to the wall. Specifically, he's been talking to the coolant line.

"—and *then* you're supposed to hold it for four seconds, not two. The manual says four. The manual has always said four. I'm not *making this up.*"

He turns. Sees you. The cloth goes over the coupling. The screwdriver goes into his pocket. His expression does a quick, efficient triage of your face and arrives at: *new information, probably not good, possibly boring.*

"Speak," he says.

You tell him. Draxen & Fould. Geological soundings. Keth-9 to asteroid cluster 4417. Twelve hours a leg. Two legs minimum. Three-fifty each. The mining company pays on schedule.

Oskar is quiet for a moment. He sets the cloth down. Wipes his hands on his coverall. Leans against the engine block, which is warm, and crosses his arms.

"Right," he says. "So. The shape of this." He counts on his fingers. "The Varga run. Three crates in the hold. Two legs. Final destination in a chit you haven't opened yet. That's a hard deadline. Nine days. The mortgage." He uncrosses. Recrosses. "Now you're adding a *survey contract* on top of a *delivery run* with *sealed cargo* that you're not allowed to describe to me."

He says *not allowed to describe to me* with a flatness that is, in Oskar, the equivalent of a shout.

"Let me do the arithmetic, Captain, because I will do it whether you want me to or not." He pulls the maintenance tablet off the engine block, turns it on, starts tapping. "The Varga run is three legs total. You've done the first — Efate. Two left. The survey is two legs. Four legs minimum before you're done with either of these. The *Kestrel* can do it. Fuel-wise, yes. Reaction mass is fine for six jumps at current load." He taps. "Time-wise, that's *eighteen to twenty-four hours of flight time* if you're doing them back-to-back. Plus port time. Plus loading and unloading. Plus the *actual* work of flying a geological survey, which is not the same as pointing a ship at a rock and calling it a job."

He sets the tablet down. Looks at you.

"Nine days. Four legs. Two different clients. One of them is a woman who told you not to open the crates and the other is a mining company that wants survey data in a specific format by a specific date." He shrugs. "It's not impossible. It's *tight.* And you have to sequence it right, or you'll be in the wrong place on the wrong day and both of them will be asking very different questions about why the *Kestrel* is late."

He picks up the cloth again. Wrings it. Sets it back down.

"So. What's the order? Survey first, then delivery? Delivery first, then survey? Are you doing them *at the same time,* which I want to point out is not a thing you do with a single-hulled free trader unless you've got a *very* confident pilot, and I have looked at you, Captain, and I have *seen* your confidence, and I respect it, but I also *fear* it."

He pauses. Then, quieter: "And the crates. They're in the hold. They're going to be in the hold for the survey legs too. I'm not asking what they are. I'm asking you to confirm, one more time, that they're *inert.* That they're just *sitting there.* Because I'm about to run a twelve-hour jump with a geological survey payload in the rear bay and *three mystery boxes* in the forward bay, and if one of those boxes starts doing *things* to the nav computer in the middle of a rock survey, I am going to be very, very *specific* about what I'm feeling."

The engine ticks. The coolant line hisses faintly, satisfied. The *Kestrel's* instruments glow green around you, all of them, all of them waiting for a vector.

"Order, Captain? And do I need to calibrate the survey array before we lift, or is that Draxen & Fould's problem?"
